stories.headline: Special Parliament session from Nov 30 amid delimitation bill buzz
stories.summary: Parliament is set to meet for a special session from November 30 to December 3, 2026, for 'Essential Government Business,' with the Lok Sabha convening on November 30 and the Rajya Sabha on December 2. The session is taking place amid speculation over a proposed delimitation bill, with both the Centre and Opposition preparing for contentious proceedings. The DMK has said it will support delimitation if Tamil Nadu's 7.2% share in Lok Sabha seats is assured. The Congress has alleged that the Monsoon Session was not formally ended because the government is seeking a majority for the delimitation bill. Questions have also been raised about whether a regular Winter Session will be held.
stories.whyItMatters: Delimitation affects federal representation, seat shares among states, and legislative arithmetic; the session tests parliamentary procedure, opposition strategy, and Centre-state equity.

static.whatIsIt: Parliament comprises the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha (Article 79); a Bill becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent (Article 111).

static.topic: Delimitation and Federal Representation
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Representation, Federalism & Constitutional Amendments
static.whatIsIt: Delimitation is the redrawing of constituency boundaries and allocation of seats to States/UTs to reflect population changes, carried out by a Delimitation Commission under Article 82 and related laws.
static.background: After the 1971 Census, delimitation was frozen until 2001 by the 42nd Amendment; the 84th Amendment (2001) froze Lok Sabha seat allocation to States until the first Census after 2026, while the 87th Amendment (2003) allowed readjustment of constituencies within States on the 2001 Census without changing seat numbers.
static.geography: Inter-state seat shares vary with population; southern and some smaller states fear relative loss of Lok Sabha seats and federal influence if seats are reallocated on current population.
static.socioEconomic: Delimitation intersects with representation of populous northern states and concerns about equitable representation across states with different demographic trajectories.
static.whyInNews: A special Parliament session is being held amid speculation over a proposed delimitation bill and DMK's demand for Tamil Nadu's 7.2% seat share.
static.wayForward: Build political consensus on population versus representation criteria, ensure transparent census and delimitation data, and address federal equity concerns.
prelimsPointers: Delimitation Commission is constituted by the President and works with the Election Commission; its orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in courts.
84th Amendment froze Lok Sabha seat allocation until the first Census after 2026.
87th Amendment allowed readjustment of constituencies within states on 2001 Census without changing total seats.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how delimitation after 2026 can balance demographic representation with federal equity and legislative scrutiny.

stories.headline: Trump's new tariff wall tests India's trade strategy and leverage
stories.summary: The United States has rolled out a fresh set of tariffs, with the Trump administration invoking Section 301 of the Trade Act, 1974 to restore duties that the US Supreme Court had struck down. India figures among the affected partners, and the proposed rates are being compared with those faced by rival exporters in ASEAN and other competing economies. New Delhi is seen as enjoying a relative cost edge over some competitors, but the uncertainty surrounding the measures is itself a bigger drag on exporters and on the pending India–US trade deal. In parallel, Washington has threatened a 40% tariff on China, signalling that tariffs remain a bargaining chip in US–China negotiations. Indian commentary broadly urges Delhi to hold its ground on the trade deal while pressing for predictability and legal durability in the tariff regime.
stories.whyItMatters: US tariff actions bear directly on India's export competitiveness, the rupee, and the stalled bilateral trade deal — a recurring GS-II/GS-III theme linking trade policy, WTO rules and strategic autonomy.

static.topic: India–US Trade Relations and Unilateral Tariff Actions
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral relations; India and global powers
static.whatIsIt: The India–US economic relationship is among India's most consequential bilateral trade links, covering goods, services, energy and defence trade. It is managed through mechanisms such as the India–US Trade Policy Forum and periodic bilateral trade negotiations, but has repeatedly been disturbed by unilateral US tariff actions.
static.background: The US imposed Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminium in 2018; India retaliated with tariffs on selected US products in 2019. The US withdrew India's GSP benefits in 2019. Both countries have litigated trade disputes at the WTO, including on solar cells and steel. A limited bilateral trade agreement has been under discussion for several years without conclusion.
static.socioEconomic: Tariff shocks fall hardest on labour-intensive export segments — textiles and apparel, gems and jewellery, marine products, auto components and engineering goods — where MSMEs and job-intensive clusters dominate. Uncertainty also affects order books, credit costs and investment planning.
static.whyInNews: The Trump administration's new Section 301 tariffs, aimed at restoring duties struck down by the US Supreme Court, directly affect Indian exports and complicate the pending India–US trade deal.
static.wayForward: India should pursue a durable, rules-based settlement rather than ad hoc concessions; diversify export markets; strengthen domestic value addition; and keep WTO options open while negotiating predictability in tariff treatment.
prelimsPointers: Section 301 of the US Trade Act, 1974 empowers the US Trade Representative to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices deemed unfair.
Section 232 tariffs rest on national-security grounds, whereas Section 301 rests on unfair-trade-practice findings.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how unilateral tariff instruments in major economies affect India's export competitiveness and strategic autonomy, and suggest a negotiating framework that balances both.

static.topic: WTO Dispute Settlement and the Challenge of Unilateral Trade Measures
static.syllabusNode: Economy — External sector; international economic institutions
static.whatIsIt: The WTO's Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU) provides a rules-based mechanism for resolving trade conflicts through panels and, ordinarily, an Appellate Body. Its paralysis has pushed countries towards unilateral measures and alternative arrangements.
static.background: The WTO was established in 1995 as the successor to GATT (1947). The Appellate Body has been unable to hear new appeals since 2019 because the US has blocked appointments of new members. In response, several members set up the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA). India has been both a frequent user and a target of the system.
static.socioEconomic: A weakened dispute settlement system raises the cost of trade for smaller exporters, who lack the bargaining power to secure bilateral carve-outs and depend on multilateral rules for predictability.
static.whyInNews: The new US tariffs, including the Section 301 action, illustrate how major economies increasingly act outside the WTO framework when multilateral remedies are unavailable.
static.wayForward: India should push for restoration of a functioning Appellate Body, use the MPIA where feasible, build coalitions with like-minded developing countries, and document violations to preserve legal options.
prelimsPointers: The WTO is headquartered in Geneva and came into being in 1995, replacing GATT.
The WTO Appellate Body has not been able to hear new appeals since 2019 due to vacant appointments.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the crisis in WTO dispute settlement has encouraged unilateral trade measures, and evaluate India's options for protecting its trade interests.

static.topic: Tariffs, Trade Diversion and India's Export Competitiveness
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Trade policy; tariffs and export competitiveness
static.whatIsIt: Tariffs alter relative prices across countries and can divert trade towards lower-tariff suppliers. India's competitiveness in labour-intensive exports is measured against peers such as Vietnam, Bangladesh, Thailand and other ASEAN economies.
static.background: India began tariff liberalisation in 1991. It signed the ASEAN–India Trade in Goods Agreement (AITIGA), in force since 2010, and is reviewing it. India opted out of the RCEP in 2019, citing concerns over Chinese goods and domestic industry impact.
static.socioEconomic: Where India faces lower relative tariffs than ASEAN rivals, it can gain orders in textiles, footwear, marine products and processed foods; but such advantages are fragile and can be reversed by a single policy change abroad.
static.whyInNews: Reports comparing India's proposed tariff treatment with that of rival nations suggest India has a relative edge in some segments — but at a cost, and amid high uncertainty.
static.wayForward: India should reduce its own input and logistics costs, deepen value addition, conclude balanced FTAs, and build export resilience so that competitiveness does not depend on another country's tariff decisions.
prelimsPointers: India is a founding member of GATT/WTO.
India opted out of the RCEP negotiations in 2019; AITIGA has been in force since 2010.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether tariff differentials alone can sustain India's export competitiveness, and outline the structural reforms needed to make export gains durable.

prelims: Section 301 of the US Trade Act, 1974 is the legal basis for the new US tariff action, used to restore duties that the US Supreme Court had struck down.
The US has separately threatened a 40% tariff on China, indicating tariffs are being used as negotiating leverage in US–China talks.

stories.mainsQuestion: Unilateral tariff actions by major economies are straining the rules-based trading order. stories.headline: AI race shifts: Nvidia export curbs, SAP job cuts, Anthropic IPO debate
stories.summary: Reports indicate SAP is considering at least 10,000 job cuts as part of an AI-driven restructuring, following executive board changes and a broader product overhaul. Separately, Nvidia has stopped shipping AI servers to buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, according to a Financial Times report, while Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters, apologised to employees and vowed to be a better CEO. Opinion pieces examine Anthropic's $1.5-trillion IPO and argue developing countries need targeted AI policies rather than blanket compute taxes or indiscriminate subsidies. Another column argues that in the AI battleground, capital follows talent and talent follows opportunity. Together, the developments highlight geopolitical export controls, corporate restructuring and the global contest for AI capacity and talent.
stories.whyItMatters: UPSC relevance: AI, export controls, tech geopolitics, employment restructuring and global governance of emerging technologies intersect with GS-II international relations, GS-III economy and science & technology. The story is useful for prelims facts and mains debates on strategic autonomy, labour markets and multilateral rule-making.

static.topic: Global AI Governance and Multilateralism

stories.headline: Myanmar refuses full compliance with ICJ genocide ruling; China faces dilemma
stories.summary: Myanmar has said it will not fully comply with the International Court of Justice's ruling holding it responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, describing the court's measures as 'inappropriate'. The judgment — reported as the first time the World Court has held a state responsible for genocide — is final and binding, but the ICJ has no police power of its own and enforcement ultimately rests with the UN Security Council, where a P5 veto can block action. The case traces back to The Gambia's 2019 application under the Genocide Convention, which produced provisional measures in 2020 and now a substantive finding. The ruling has also created a diplomatic problem for China, Myanmar's closest strategic partner and a major investor in Rakhine State, where the atrocities occurred.
stories.whyItMatters: It is a live test case for the enforcement limits of international law and the UN collective security architecture — a recurring UPSC theme linking global governance, the Genocide Convention and P5 veto politics. It also directly touches India's neighbourhood, refugee and Rohingya policy.

perspectives.take: Leads on Myanmar's defiant official response, framing the ruling as a state rejecting what it calls 'inappropriate' international measures — a sovereignty-versus-accountability angle.
Sober, legal-institutional framing: stresses the landmark nature of the finding (first state held responsible for genocide) while foregrounding the near-total absence of enforcement mechanisms.

static.topic: International Court of Justice and the Genocide Convention
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and International Institutions
static.whatIsIt: The ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, seated at the Peace Palace in The Hague. It settles legal disputes between states and gives advisory opinions to UN organs. The 1948 Genocide Convention criminalises genocide under international law and, through its Article IX, allows disputes over its interpretation or application to be referred to the ICJ.
static.background: The ICJ was established in 1945 under the UN Charter and functions under its own Statute. The Genocide Convention was adopted in 1948 and entered into force in 1951. The Gambia filed proceedings against Myanmar in November 2019 alleging violations of the Convention, and the ICJ indicated provisional measures in January 2020. The current judgment is reported as the first instance of the World Court holding a state responsible for genocide; earlier cases such as Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia dealt with failure to prevent genocide rather than direct responsibility.
static.geography: Peace Palace, The Hague, Netherlands. The ICJ is distinct from the International Criminal Court, also in The Hague, which tries individuals under the Rome Statute.
static.whyInNews: Myanmar has declared it will not fully comply with the ICJ's orders, and the ruling is final but practically unenforceable without Security Council backing.
static.wayForward: Debate typically centres on strengthening compliance mechanisms, expanding the use of advisory opinions, and reforming the Security Council veto in mass-atrocity situations — none of which is easily achievable given P5 interests.
prelimsPointers: The ICJ has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms by the UN General Assembly and Security Council voting concurrently.
Only states may be parties to contentious cases before the ICJ; individuals are tried by the ICC.
Under Article 94 of the UN Charter, compliance with ICJ judgments may be referred to the Security Council, where any permanent member can veto action.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether the ICJ's genocide jurisprudence can deliver accountability when enforcement depends on a veto-bound Security Council.

static.topic: Rohingya Crisis and India's Refugee Policy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood; also Internal Security (GS-III) — border management and refugees
static.whatIsIt: The Rohingya are a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority concentrated in Myanmar's Rakhine State. Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law effectively excluded them from citizenship, rendering most stateless and exposing them to decades of systematic discrimination and violence.
static.background: Persecution and periodic displacement have recurred since the 1970s and 1980s. Large-scale military 'clearance operations' in 2017 drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya across the border, overwhelmingly into Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar district. The Gambia's ICJ case followed in 2019. India, which hosts a smaller Rohingya refugee population, has faced Supreme Court litigation over proposed deportations. India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol and has no dedicated domestic refugee law; refugees are dealt with under the Foreigners Act, 1946 and the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920.
static.geography: Rakhine State lies on Myanmar's western coast, bordering Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal; Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh hosts the largest refugee settlement complex.
static.socioEconomic: Statelessness denies the Rohingya formal education, healthcare access, freedom of movement and lawful livelihoods, entrenching intergenerational poverty and dependence on humanitarian aid.
static.whyInNews: The ICJ genocide ruling against Myanmar revives questions about accountability, refugee returns and the obligations of host and transit states, including India.
static.wayForward: Commonly suggested measures include a domestic refugee and asylum law, a clear non-refoulement framework, and regional burden-sharing with Bangladesh and ASEAN partners.
prelimsPointers: India is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention or the 1967 Protocol and has no standalone refugee legislation.
The Rohingya were effectively stripped of citizenship by Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law.
Rakhine State borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal, and most Rohingya refugees fled to Cox's Bazar.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether India's absence of a refugee law is sustainable given protracted displacement in its neighbourhood.

static.topic: China's Strategic and Economic Stakes in Myanmar and Rakhine
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World; Major Powers and their Neighbourhood Policies
static.whatIsIt: China is Myanmar's largest trading partner, principal arms supplier and most important diplomatic shield. Its interests in Rakhine State include the Kyaukphyu deep-sea port and the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), a Belt and Road Initiative project linking landlocked Yunnan to the Indian Ocean.
static.background: Twin oil and gas pipelines running from Kyaukphyu to Kunming have operated since the 2010s, giving China an energy route that bypasses the Malacca Strait. The CMEC was agreed in 2017 as part of the BRI. China has repeatedly shielded Myanmar from concerted Security Council action, including after the 2021 coup, and has engaged the junta bilaterally while ASEAN pursued its Five-Point Consensus.
static.geography: Kyaukphyu sits on the Bay of Bengal coast in Rakhine State; the corridor runs north to Yunnan province, giving China direct access to the Indian Ocean.
static.socioEconomic: Chinese-backed infrastructure is central to Rakhine's economy but has been criticised for displacement, opaque financing and limited local benefit, feeding resentment in a conflict-affected region.
static.whyInNews: The ICJ genocide ruling places Beijing in a dilemma: endorsing accountability would undercut a strategic partner and jeopardise Rakhine investments, while opposing it invites criticism over mass-atrocity complicity.
prelimsPointers: The China-Myanmar Economic Corridor links Kunming in Yunnan to Kyaukphyu on the Bay of Bengal.
Oil and gas pipelines from Kyaukphyu to Kunming give China an Indian Ocean energy route bypassing the Malacca Strait.
ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus, adopted in 2021, remains the regional framework for addressing the Myanmar crisis.
static.mainsAngle: Assess how China's economic and strategic interests in Myanmar constrain multilateral accountability for mass atrocities.

ICJ judgments are binding but enforcement under Article 94 of the UN Charter runs through the Security Council, where any P5 member can veto action.
Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law rendered the Rohingya effectively stateless; large-scale displacement followed military operations in Rakhine State in 2017.
India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol and governs refugees under the Foreigners Act, 1946 and the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920.
stories.mainsQuestion: The ICJ's genocide ruling against Myanmar exposes the gap between international legal pronouncements and their enforcement. Examine the limits of the UN collective security architecture in this light, and discuss the implications for India's refugee and neighbourhood policy.

stories.headline: Houthi strikes, Kuwait drone attack escalate West Asia tensions; oil gains
stories.summary: Two separate escalations unfolded across West Asia on the same day, per the reports dated 26 November 2026. Yemen's Houthis struck Saudi oil infrastructure, including refinery-linked targets, while the Saudi-led coalition hit the Houthi-held capital Sana'a — exchanges that reporting describes as near-daily in Yemen's revived civil war. Separately, Iranian-made drones struck Kuwaiti military installations, including an air-defence detection station, killing two Italian technicians of the defence firm Rheinmetall and injuring two others; Kuwait blamed Iran for the strike on what its military called a "vital" facility, a charge conveyed by Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani. Crude markets reacted immediately, with oil extending gains on Middle East tensions and traders in the bunker and crude segment flagging supply-shortage concerns after strikes near Hormuz and in Saudi Arabia.
stories.whyItMatters: The story sits at the intersection of GS-II (West Asia geopolitics, India's extended neighbourhood, multilateral mediation) and GS-III (energy security, chokepoint vulnerability, maritime trade), while the chokepoint map — Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb — is recurring prelims material.

perspectives.take: Indian-audience commentary framing (YouTube short, opinionated): reads the Saudi refinery strike primarily through oil and trade risk for India rather than regional politics.

Wire-style factual reporting; attributes the Kuwait strike details to Italian FM Tajani and separately notes that Houthi–Saudi coalition exchanges have become near-daily, avoiding blame attribution of its own.
Business-desk lens: leads with casualty figures and Kuwait's formal attribution of blame to Iran, implicitly flagging Gulf investment and expatriate-security risk.
Western security framing: couples the Houthi strike on Saudi oil infrastructure with Riyadh's intensified campaign in Yemen, presenting it as a two-way escalation cycle.
Markets-first framing: treats oil price gains as the headline consequence, positioning the Gulf as a risk premium rather than a political story.
Shipping-and-fuel trade lens: foregrounds supply-shortage concerns and the Hormuz dimension, i.e., physical flow disruption rather than price sentiment.

static.topic: West Asian Escalation and India's Stakes
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World; Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: The current round of conflict involving Houthi strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure, Saudi-led coalition strikes on Houthi-held Sana'a, and an Iranian-made drone attack on Kuwaiti military installations that killed two Italian defence-firm technicians. It marks a widening of the theatre beyond Yemen to Gulf states and foreign personnel on Gulf soil.
static.background: Yemen's civil war escalated after the Houthis — a Zaidi Shia movement from northern Yemen — took Sana'a in 2014; a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 reduced but did not end hostilities, and fighting has revived. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and Red Sea shipping have recurred since 2019, with a sharp upsurge after October 2023. Kuwait, a GCC member, hosts foreign defence contractors and US military facilities, making it a sensitive target set.
static.geography: West Asia: Yemen (Sana'a, Houthi-held north) and Saudi Arabia in the south-western Arabian Peninsula; Kuwait at the head of the Persian Gulf, bordering Iraq and Saudi Arabia.
static.socioEconomic: Gulf states host large expatriate workforces, including about nine million Indians, whose remittances are a major external-sector support for India. Attacks on Gulf soil raise insurance, aviation-routing and investment risk, and can push up crude import bills and domestic inflation in importing economies like India.
static.whyInNews: Same-day reports of Houthi strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure, coalition strikes on Sana'a, and an Iranian drone attack in Kuwait that killed two Italian civilians.
static.wayForward: India's interest lies in de-escalation diplomacy — engaging Riyadh, Tehran and Gulf capitals, supporting UN-led mediation, protecting its diaspora through embassy advisories, and diversifying both crude sourcing and routing.
prelimsPointers: The Houthis are a Zaidi Shia movement that seized Yemen's capital Sana'a in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition intervention in 2015.
Kuwait is a GCC member state hosting US military facilities and foreign defence contractors.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate how renewed West Asian conflict affects India's energy security, diaspora safety and diplomatic balancing between Riyadh, Tehran and the wider Gulf.

static.topic: Strait of Hormuz, Bab-el-Mandeb and India's Energy Security
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Infrastructure: Energy; Security — maritime security and chokepoints
static.whatIsIt: The two maritime chokepoints through which most West Asian crude and LNG reach world markets. Any credible threat near them — as suggested by the reported strike context and supply-shortage concerns in crude trading — transmits directly into freight, insurance and landed fuel costs.
static.background: Hormuz has been a flashpoint since the 1980s 'Tanker War'; Indian Navy escort operations in the Gulf of Oman and Persian Gulf have been conducted under Operation Sankalp since 2019, and anti-piracy/escort deployments were extended to the Gulf of Aden and Red Sea after attacks on merchant shipping. India is a founding member of the IMO framework and participates in regional maritime-security coordination.
static.geography: Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman; Iran lies to the north and Oman/UAE (Musandam exclave) to the south, with the strait narrowing to roughly 30-plus km and shipping confined to designated lanes. Bab-el-Mandeb, between Yemen and the Horn of Africa, links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Suez route.
static.socioEconomic: A very large share of global seaborne petroleum liquids passes through Hormuz, and India sources a substantial part of its crude from West Asia — Iraq, Saudi Arabia, UAE and Kuwait — besides Russia. Disruption raises India's import bill, current-account pressure and retail fuel and fertiliser costs, and lengthens voyage times for Red Sea traffic.
static.whyInNews: Crude markets extended gains and bunker/crude traders flagged supply-shortage concerns after strikes near Hormuz and in Saudi Arabia.
static.wayForward: Build strategic petroleum reserves and diversify crude sources, deepen the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor and Chabahar/INSTC connectivity options, and sustain Indian Navy maritime-domain awareness and escort deployments.
prelimsPointers: Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman; Bab-el-Mandeb links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
The Indian Navy's maritime-security deployment in the Gulf region is called Operation Sankalp.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how chokepoint vulnerability in West Asia shapes India's energy security calculus and what hedging instruments India can deploy.

static.topic: UN Security Council and Conflict Mediation in West Asia
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance; UN and multilateral reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN framework within which West Asian conflicts are debated and mediated, and whose paralysis on such conflicts drives the debate on Security Council reform. The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members serving two-year terms.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 — India, Brazil, Germany, Japan — campaigns for Security Council expansion, while the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on reform remain inconclusive; Africa's Ezulwini Consensus is a key reference point. P5 veto politics has repeatedly stymied Council action on West Asian conflicts.
static.geography: UN headquarters in New York; the International Court of Justice sits at The Hague.
static.socioEconomic: Council inaction shifts conflict management to regional organisations, ad hoc coalitions and bilateral mediation, raising costs for trade-dependent states including India.
static.whyInNews: Escalation across Yemen, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait renews questions about the Security Council's capacity to mediate and about the legitimacy of its present composition.
static.wayForward: India can press for text-based negotiations in the IGN, align with G4 and African positions, and continue UN peacekeeping contributions as evidence of systemic stakeholding.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent and 10 elected for two-year terms.
The ICJ is at The Hague and the UN headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: Assess how repeated P5 vetoes on West Asian conflicts strengthen the case for UNSC reform and what India's strategy in the IGN should be.

prelims: Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman; Bab-el-Mandeb links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden — both are critical global oil chokepoints.
The Houthis (Ansar Allah) are a Zaidi Shia movement that captured Yemen's capital Sana'a in 2014, leading to a Saudi-led coalition intervention in 2015.
Kuwait is a GCC member state that hosts foreign defence contractors and US military installations, which is why strikes there draw wider international casualties.
The Indian Navy's Gulf-region maritime security deployment is called Operation Sankalp.
stories.mainsQuestion: The widening of conflict in West Asia — from Yemen and Saudi Arabia to Kuwait — poses a compound challenge to India's energy security, diaspora protection and strategic balancing. Examine, and suggest a calibrated Indian response.

stories.headline: Tamil Nadu's defiance of Supreme Court order on Thirupparankundram Deepathoon ritual
stories.summary: The Supreme Court allowed the lighting of the 'Deepathoon' at the Thirupparankundram hill temple near Madurai as a one-time measure during the Karthigai Deepam festival, treating it as an interim accommodation rather than a recognition of any customary right. The Tamil Nadu government's handling of the ritual, and its apparent backing of the Deepathoon claim against the court's direction, has drawn sharp criticism from editorialists who argue that a state cannot pick and choose which judicial orders to obey. Commentators warn that executive non-compliance erodes the rule of law and invites contempt proceedings, and note that the dispute has acquired a political and communal dimension in southern Tamil Nadu. The Indian Express editorial urges Chief Minister Vijay to appear before the court and build political consensus instead of confronting the judiciary.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the constitutional duty of state authorities to comply with judicial orders (Articles 141 and 144) and the scope of contempt powers — a recurring UPSC theme on judicial supremacy versus executive autonomy. It also links festival and temple administration to questions of law and order and secular governance.

perspectives.take: Calls the state's position indefensible: Tamil Nadu should have complied with the court's order rather than backing the Deepathoon claim, framing it as a rule-of-law failure.

static.topic: Judicial review and executive compliance with court orders
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts & Judicial Review
static.whatIsIt: The power of constitutional courts to test executive and legislative action against the Constitution, coupled with the duty of all authorities to act in aid of the Supreme Court's orders.
static.background: Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) provide writ jurisdiction; the collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine; PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s.
static.whyInNews: The Tamil Nadu government's alleged defiance of the Supreme Court's order permitting the Deepathoon at Thirupparankundram as a one-time measure has revived debate on executive compliance with judicial directions.
static.wayForward: States should comply first and contest later through review or curative petitions; courts should use contempt powers sparingly but firmly, while governments build political consensus on sensitive ritual disputes.

static.topic: Thirupparankundram temple and Karthigai Deepam
static.syllabusNode: Art & Culture — Temple architecture, festivals and heritage
static.whatIsIt: Thirupparankundram, near Madurai, is one of the six abodes (Arupadai Veedu) of Lord Murugan and a rock-cut hill temple; Karthigai Deepam is a Tamil festival of lights observed in the Tamil month of Karthigai.
static.background: ASI protects monuments under the AMASR Act 1958; India has 40+ UNESCO World Heritage Sites; the eight classical dances were codified by the Sangeet Natak Akademi.
static.geography: Thirupparankundram hill, Madurai district, southern Tamil Nadu.
static.socioEconomic: Temple festivals are major local economic and social events; disputes over ritual rights can sharpen religious and caste fault lines.
static.whyInNews: The Deepathoon ritual at the temple during Karthigai Deepam became the subject of a Supreme Court order and a stand-off with the state government.
static.wayForward: Ritual disputes are best settled through statutory temple administration and court-supervised mechanisms rather than political mobilisation.
prelimsPointers: Dravida style: gopuram, vimana, shikhara over the sanctum.
Nagara: curvilinear shikhara; Odisha, Khajuraho and Solanki are sub-styles.
static.mainsAngle: Heritage conservation versus urbanisation and cultural diplomacy as soft power — and the management of religious festivals as sites of social and legal contestation.

stories.headline: Opposition escalates anti-SIR, CEC protests as poll season nears
stories.summary: Opposition parties have escalated their campaign against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and over the functioning of the Election Commission, with the I.N.D.I.A. bloc planning major rallies in Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and West Bengal after a protest in Delhi. In West Bengal, police reportedly visited people whose names had been deleted from the rolls to collect details, prompting the Opposition to ask under what legal authority such visits were being made. A separate report said roughly one in three transgender voters had disappeared from the electoral rolls, sharpening concerns that the revision is falling hardest on marginalised groups. Roll revision is carried out under the ECI's constitutional mandate in Article 324 and the Representation of the People Act, 1950, and Section 22 of that Act requires notice and a hearing before a name is deleted.
stories.whyItMatters: Electoral roll revision sits at the intersection of the ECI's constitutional powers, the right to franchise and federal politics — a recurring theme in Prelims (Article 324, RPA 1950/1951) and in GS-II questions on the independence of constitutional bodies.

perspectives.take: A ground-level Kolkata report: police visiting deleted electors, framed around the Opposition's demand to know the legal basis for such verification.

static.topic: Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Electoral Rolls
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Elections; Constitutional Bodies; Representation of the People Act, 1950
static.whatIsIt: SIR is an intensive, door-to-door verification exercise conducted by the Election Commission of India to clean up electoral rolls, in which enumerators visit electors, collect and cross-check details, and identify dead, shifted, duplicated or otherwise ineligible entries. Names that cannot be verified may be deleted after following the prescribed procedure.
static.background: Electoral rolls are prepared and revised under the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, with the ECI conducting annual and quarterly revisions. A special intensive revision is a more exhaustive exercise than the routine revision. Section 22 of the RPA, 1950 governs deletion of names and requires that an elector be given notice and an opportunity of hearing before removal. The ECI's superintendence and control over the preparation of rolls flows from Article 324.
static.geography: Conducted state-wise; the current controversy centres on West Bengal, while the Opposition's protest rallies are planned in Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and West Bengal.
static.socioEconomic: Deletions tend to fall disproportionately on the poor, migrants, homeless persons, transgender persons and those lacking documentary proof of residence, raising the risk of large-scale disenfranchisement of already marginalised groups.
static.whyInNews: Opposition parties allege arbitrary deletions; in West Bengal, police reportedly visited persons deleted from the rolls seeking details, and the Opposition has questioned the legal basis for such visits.
static.wayForward: A transparent, publicly notified deletion process with mandatory notice and hearing; accessible grievance redress through Form 6, Form 7 and Form 8 and the ECI's online portal; proactive enrolment drives for marginalised groups; and publication of disaggregated deletion data for public scrutiny.
prelimsPointers: Electoral rolls are prepared under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, while the conduct of elections is governed by the RPA, 1951.
Section 22 of the RPA, 1950 requires notice and a hearing before a name is deleted from the electoral roll.
The ECI's superintendence, direction and control of electoral roll preparation derives from Article 324.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether intensive roll-revision exercises strengthen electoral integrity or risk large-scale disenfranchisement of marginalised voters; suggest procedural safeguards.

static.topic: Election Commission of India and Appointment of the CEC
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Constitutional Bodies; Appointment to Constitutional Posts
static.whatIsIt: The ECI is a constitutional body under Article 324 that superintends, directs and controls elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. It consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners.
static.background: Article 324 provides for the ECI; the body became multi-member in 1993 with the appointment of two additional Election Commissioners. In Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023), the Supreme Court directed that appointments be made on the advice of a committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice of India. The CEC and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 subsequently codified a selection committee of the Prime Minister, a Union Minister and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha. The CEC can be removed only in the same manner and on the same grounds as a judge of the Supreme Court; other Election Commissioners are removed on the recommendation of the CEC.
static.socioEconomic: The perceived independence of the poll body is central to public confidence in elections and to the legitimacy of outcomes, making appointment and removal procedures a live political issue.
static.whyInNews: Opposition parties have combined their protest against SIR with demands relating to the neutrality of the Election Commission and the process by which the CEC is appointed, ahead of upcoming state elections.
static.wayForward: Ensure transparent and publicly defensible selection criteria, consider a fixed and secure tenure and independent funding for the ECI, and strengthen institutional safeguards against executive influence, as recommended by various committees.
prelimsPointers: The ECI is established under Article 324 and became a three-member body in 1993.
The CEC can be removed only in the same manner and on the same grounds as a judge of the Supreme Court.
Appointments to the ECI are governed by the CEC and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the constitutional safeguards for the independence of the Election Commission and evaluate whether the present appointment mechanism is adequate.

static.topic: Transgender Persons' Inclusion in Electoral Rolls
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Rights of Vulnerable Sections; Representation and Franchise
static.whatIsIt: Transgender persons in India may enrol as electors under the 'third gender' category in the electoral rolls, following judicial recognition of transgender identity and subsequent legislation.
static.background: In NALSA v. Union of India (2014), the Supreme Court recognised transgender persons as a 'third gender' and directed the State to treat them as socially and educationally backward. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 followed, prohibiting discrimination and providing for identity certificates. The ECI has since provided a third-gender option in enrolment forms.
static.socioEconomic: Transgender persons face documentation barriers, migration, family rejection and social stigma, which make them especially vulnerable to exclusion from the rolls and to being unable to prove residence during verification.
static.whyInNews: A report highlighted that a large share of transgender voters — reported as roughly one in three — had disappeared from the electoral rolls, raising concerns about exclusion during the ongoing revision exercise.
static.wayForward: Simplified documentation, community-based verification, dedicated enrolment camps, and publication of disaggregated data on transgender electors to enable monitoring of inclusion.
prelimsPointers: The Supreme Court in NALSA v. Union of India (2014) recognised transgender persons as a third gender.
The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 prohibits discrimination and provides for identity certificates.
Electoral enrolment forms provide a third-gender option for transgender electors.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the barriers to electoral participation faced by transgender persons and suggest measures to make the electoral roll process inclusive.

stories.mainsQuestion: The integrity of the electoral roll is central to free and fair elections, yet intensive revision exercises can exclude the most marginalised. stories.headline: Siang dam protests and India's border infrastructure gap with China
stories.summary: A court in Arunachal Pradesh has released two more activists detained during protests against the proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, observing that at most a case of mischief is made out. The project, planned on the Siang — the upper Brahmaputra — is promoted by the Centre as a strategic counter to China's mega hydropower development on the Yarlung Tsangpo at Medog, but faces sustained resistance from Siang valley communities over displacement, land and ecological risk. Opinion commentary in The Hindu frames the dam as emblematic of how India-China rivalry imposes costs on frontier communities and ecosystems, while a companion piece argues India needs a coordinated, long-term frontier development strategy rather than reactive projects. Together the coverage links a local agitation, hydropower policy and the wider border infrastructure contest with China.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the balance between strategic infrastructure along the LAC and environmental and community safeguards — a recurring GS-II (India-China) and GS-III (environment, infrastructure) theme. The Siang case is a ready example for questions on transboundary rivers, frontier development and hydropower trade-offs.

perspectives.take: Reports the court's bail order and the release of Siang activists, foregrounding the legal and civil-liberties dimension of the anti-dam agitation rather than the strategic rationale for the project.
Argues the Siang hydroproject shows how India-China geopolitical rivalry is being played out at the expense of local communities and fragile Himalayan ecosystems.
Calls on India to move beyond reactive, event-driven projects towards a coordinated, long-term frontier development strategy to take on China.

static.topic: India-China Border Infrastructure and Frontier Development
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its neighbourhood; bilateral relations with China
static.whatIsIt: India's programme of roads, tunnels, bridges, helipads and model villages along the Line of Actual Control, executed mainly by the Border Roads Organisation and supported by schemes such as the Border Area Development Programme and the Vibrant Villages Programme.
static.background: The build-up accelerated after the 2017 Doklam standoff and the 2020 Galwan clash. The Vibrant Villages Programme (2023) targets development of villages along the northern border, and the Sela Tunnel in Arunachal Pradesh was inaugurated in 2024. India and China reached a patrolling arrangement in October 2024 covering Depsang and Demchok.
static.geography: The LAC runs roughly 3,488 km across the Western (Ladakh), Middle (Himachal Pradesh–Uttarakhand) and Eastern (Sikkim–Arunachal Pradesh) sectors; Arunachal Pradesh accounts for the longest stretch.
static.socioEconomic: Frontier roads and villages improve connectivity, service delivery and livelihood access, but raise land acquisition, displacement and ecological concerns in sparsely populated hill districts.
static.whyInNews: Opinion commentary argues India's border infrastructure remains reactive and needs a long-term strategy; the Siang project is presented as part of the strategic response to Chinese upstream development.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise a long-term frontier development plan with stable funding, environmental safeguards, genuine community consultation and inter-agency coordination rather than project-by-project responses.

static.topic: Transboundary Rivers: Siang, Brahmaputra and China's Medog Dam
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Transboundary rivers and India-China relations
static.whatIsIt: The Siang is the Arunachal Pradesh stretch of the Yarlung Tsangpo after it enters India near Tuting. The proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project is a mega multipurpose hydropower scheme on this stretch, promoted in part as a strategic counter to Chinese upstream development.
static.background: China has built a series of run-of-the-river and storage dams on the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet; in December 2024 it approved the Medog hydropower project, reported to be the world's largest, located near the Indian border. India has consistently raised concerns about data sharing and prior consultation, and the two sides operate an MoU on hydrological data sharing. The Brahmaputra is a major transboundary river for India and Bangladesh.
static.geography: The Yarlung Tsangpo rises in the Tibetan plateau, flows east and takes a sharp bend before entering India in Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang (also called Dihang); after the Dibang and Lohit join it at Sadiya, it becomes the Brahmaputra.
static.socioEconomic: Siang valley communities depend on the river for farming, fishing and cultural life; large dams imply displacement, submergence of land and altered flow regimes downstream.
static.whyInNews: Protests against the Siang project, the arrest of activists and their subsequent release on bail, alongside opinion pieces debating strategic ambition versus ecological fallout.
static.wayForward: Basin-level cumulative impact assessment, transparent benefit-sharing, free prior informed consent of affected communities, and institutionalised transboundary data-sharing and consultation with China.

static.topic: Himalayan Hydropower and Ecological Risk

static.whatIsIt: Large hydropower projects in the seismically active eastern Himalaya raise risks of landslides, reservoir-induced seismicity, biodiversity loss and downstream flow alteration. static.background: India's hydropower push in Arunachal Pradesh dates to the 2000s. India's conservation framework rests on the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, the Biological Diversity Act 2002 and the Forest Conservation Act 1980, alongside the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) and its Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022).

static.whyInNews: The ecological fallout of the Siang project is being debated in opinion pages amid continuing local protests.
static.wayForward: Cumulative impact assessment and strategic environmental assessment at the river-basin scale, with mandatory community consent and independent monitoring.
prelimsPointers: India's biodiversity hotspots include the Himalaya and Indo-Burma.
The eastern Himalaya falls in the highest seismic zone of India.
static.mainsAngle: Balancing hydropower expansion with ecological security and community rights in the eastern Himalaya: discuss with reference to the Siang project.

static.topic: Uniform Civil Code

static.whatIsIt: A common set of civil laws applicable to all citizens in matters of marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption and succession, as envisioned in Article 44 of the Constitution.

static.topic: Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas)
static.syllabusNode: Indian Constitution — Historical Underpinnings, Significant Provisions
static.whatIsIt: 26 November is observed as Constitution Day to mark the adoption of the Constitution of India by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949; it came into force on 26 January 1950.
static.background: The Constituent Assembly, constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946, held its first sitting on 9 December 1946 and adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949, taking 2 years, 11 months and 18 days. The Government of India notified 26 November as Constitution Day in 2015, the 125th birth anniversary year of B.R. Ambedkar, who chaired the Drafting Committee.
static.socioEconomic: Constitution Day is used to promote constitutional literacy through Preamble readings and outreach by the Ministry of Law and Justice and educational institutions.
static.whyInNews: Constitution Day 2026 was marked by parliamentary programming and by the inauguration of India's first Chief Justices of India Museum.
static.wayForward: Move beyond ceremonial observance towards sustained civic education, accessible constitutional texts and Preamble reading in schools and colleges.

Constitution Day was notified in 2015, the 125th birth anniversary year of B.R. Ambedkar.
The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to frame the Constitution.

static.topic: Ambedkar's Constitutional Morality and Social Democracy
static.syllabusNode: Indian Constitution — Features, Amendments, Significant Provisions; Social Justice
static.whatIsIt: Ambedkar's argument that political democracy is incomplete without social democracy, and that constitutional forms survive only when worked with a spirit of constitutional morality and public conscience.
static.background: In the Constituent Assembly, Ambedkar cautioned that however good a Constitution may be, it may turn out bad if those who work it are a bad lot, and stressed that political democracy must be accompanied by social democracy — a way of life recognising liberty, equality and fraternity. He invoked constitutional morality, a concept associated with the historian George Grote, meaning adherence to constitutional forms and the spirit behind them.
static.socioEconomic: Directly linked to caste inequality and untouchability, and to the constitutional promise of equality of status and opportunity under Articles 14 to 17.
static.whyInNews: An explainer published on Constitution Day revisited Ambedkar's idea that democracy needs a conscience, not just a Constitution.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise constitutional morality through civic education, ethical conduct in legislatures and courts, and public scrutiny of institutional functioning.
prelimsPointers: B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly.
Ambedkar described Article 32 (constitutional remedies) as the heart and soul of the Constitution.
The phrase constitutional morality is associated with the historian George Grote.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the idea of constitutional morality shapes the working of India's democratic institutions.

static.topic: Directive Principles and the Quest for Socio-Economic Justice
static.syllabusNode: Directive Principles of State Policy; Welfare Schemes and Social Justice
static.whatIsIt: Part IV (Articles 36–51) directs the State to secure social and economic justice; the Preamble's triad of justice — social, economic and political — frames this constitutional goal.
static.background: Inspired in part by the Irish Constitution, the Directive Principles are non-justiciable but fundamental in the governance of the country under Article 37. Key provisions include Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), Article 41 (right to work, education and public assistance), Article 43 (living wage), Article 46 (educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes) and Article 47 (public health). Courts have read several Directive Principles into the fundamental rights, especially Article 21.
static.socioEconomic: Directive Principles underpin welfare legislation such as the National Food Security Act and legal-aid frameworks, and are measured through social development indicators.
static.whyInNews: A Constitution Day op-ed argued that the quest for social and economic justice runs through the very fabric of the Constitution.
static.wayForward: Use the Directive Principles as a governance audit framework, tracking outcomes in health, education and livelihood rather than mere legislative enactment.
prelimsPointers: Directive Principles are contained in Part IV, Articles 36 to 51.
Article 39A provides for equal justice and free legal aid.
Under Article 37, Directive Principles are non-justiciable but fundamental in the governance of the country.
static.mainsAngle: The Directive Principles are described as the conscience of the Constitution — discuss their role in realising socio-economic justice in India.

stories.headline: SC quashes Bihar remission; HC on AI authorship; journalist protection in focus
stories.summary: A clutch of court developments on the same day spanned criminal remission, corruption trials, copyright and press freedom. The Supreme Court quashed the Bihar government's remission order in favour of former MP Anand Mohan, convicted in the 1994 murder of IAS officer G. Krishnaiah, restoring the sentence in a case where the state's exercise of executive clemency had been under challenge. Separately, the Delhi High Court upheld the framing of corruption charges against former Bihar Chief Minister Lalu Prasad Yadav, Rabri Devi and others in the IRCTC scam, refusing to interfere at the charge stage. In a third matter, the Delhi High Court agreed to examine whether an artificial intelligence system can be recognised as an 'author' under the Copyright Act. On press freedom, the Supreme Court said it will examine who qualifies as a journalist for protection, and referred complaints of alleged detention and assault of seven journalists during Delhi protests to a high-powered committee, with a Bench remarking that self-proclaimed journalists may not enjoy the same protection as accredited ones.
stories.whyItMatters: The set ties together judicial review of executive remission, the standard for interference at the charge-framing stage, the unsettled interface of AI with copyright law, and the scope of Article 19(1)(a) protection for the press — all recurring UPSC themes in polity, governance and rights.

static.topic: Judicial review of executive remission and the supervisory role of the higher judiciary
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts & Judicial Review
static.whatIsIt: Remission is the reduction of a sentence already awarded, exercised by the appropriate government under the criminal procedure law and, in certain cases, by the President (Art. 72) or Governor (Art. 161). Such executive orders are subject to judicial review on grounds of arbitrariness, non-application of mind, or disregard of the sentencing court's opinion and the victim's family.
static.background: The Supreme Court is the apex court under Article 124 and High Courts under Article 214; judicial review is the power to test executive and legislative action against the Constitution. The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998), and Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. Writ jurisdiction lies under Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC); Article 142 gives the Supreme Court power to do complete justice. PILs from the late 1970s widened access to justice.
static.socioEconomic: Remission decisions in high-profile cases raise questions of equality before law, political influence on executive clemency, and the rights of victims' families.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court quashed the Bihar government's remission granted to former MP Anand Mohan in the 1994 murder of IAS officer G. Krishnaiah.
static.wayForward: Codify clear, reasoned criteria and mandatory recording of reasons for remission, ensure the sentencing court's opinion and victim-hearing are on record, and publish remission orders to make the exercise transparent and reviewable.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court lies in disputes between the Centre and states (Article 131); advisory jurisdiction under Article 143.
Pardoning power of the Governor (Art. 161) does not extend to court-martial sentences, which fall under the President's power (Art. 72).
static.mainsAngle: Examine how far courts may review executive remission. Does judicial supervision strengthen the rule of law or encroach on constitutionally conferred clemency powers?

static.topic: Artificial intelligence and authorship under copyright law
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology / Economy — Intellectual Property Rights: Copyright and emerging technologies
static.whatIsIt: Copyright protects original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works. The 'author' is the person who creates the work, and Indian law presumes a human creator; whether a machine-generated output can have an author, and who owns it, is legally unsettled.
static.background: India's copyright framework dates to the Copyright Act, 1957, which has been amended several times, most significantly in 2012 to align with international norms and to address digital and internet-era issues. India is a member of the Berne Convention and the TRIPS Agreement. Globally, courts and offices have taken divergent views on AI-generated works, with some jurisdictions requiring human authorship.
static.socioEconomic: Generative AI raises questions of ownership, licensing of training data, remuneration for human creators, and liability for infringing outputs.
static.whyInNews: The Delhi High Court has agreed to examine whether AI can be recognised as an author under the Copyright Act.
static.wayForward: Await judicial clarification while considering a calibrated statutory framework that distinguishes AI-assisted works from fully autonomous output, addresses training-data licensing, and protects human creators' livelihoods.
prelimsPointers: Copyright in India is governed by the Copyright Act, 1957, administered by the Copyright Office under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade.
India is a signatory to the Berne Convention and the TRIPS Agreement, which set minimum standards for protection of works.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the challenges that generative artificial intelligence poses to the concept of authorship and ownership in copyright law. What principles should guide reform?

static.topic: Press freedom, journalist accreditation and Article 19(1)(a)
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Fundamental Rights: Freedom of Speech and Expression; Role of the Press
static.whatIsIt: Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) includes the freedom of the press; reasonable restrictions may be imposed under Article 19(2). Accreditation is an administrative recognition granted to media persons, distinct from the constitutional right itself.
static.background: Press freedom has been read into Article 19(1)(a) since the early years of the Constitution, and the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the press is a pillar of democracy and a check on government. Statutory and administrative schemes for accreditation of journalists exist at the central and state levels, and the Press Council of India, a statutory body, oversees press standards.
static.socioEconomic: With digital and independent media expanding, the line between accredited and non-accredited journalists affects access, safety and the practical ability to report on protests and unrest.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court said it will examine who qualifies as a journalist for protection, and referred complaints of alleged detention and assault of seven journalists during Delhi protests to a high-powered committee.
static.wayForward: Ensure that safety and constitutional protection attach to the act of journalism rather than to accreditation status alone, while making accreditation transparent, inclusive of digital media, and free of political discretion.
prelimsPointers: Freedom of the press is not a separate fundamental right but is read into Article 19(1)(a).
The Press Council of India is a statutory, quasi-judicial body that adjudicates complaints against the press and protects journalistic freedom.
static.mainsAngle: Should constitutional protection for journalists depend on accreditation? Examine in the light of Article 19(1)(a) and the changing media landscape.

prelims: The Supreme Court quashed the Bihar government's remission order in the Anand Mohan case, reaffirming that executive remission is subject to judicial review.
The Delhi High Court upheld the framing of corruption charges against Lalu Prasad Yadav, Rabri Devi and others in the IRCTC scam, declining to interfere at the charge stage.
The Delhi High Court will examine whether an AI system can be recognised as an 'author' under the Copyright Act, 1957.

The Supreme Court referred complaints of alleged detention and assault of seven journalists during Delhi protests to a high-powered committee, while examining who qualifies as a journalist for protection.
stories.mainsQuestion: Judicial review of executive remission, the definition of authorship in copyright law, and the scope of protection for journalists all test the balance between constitutional rights and institutional discretion. Examine, with recent examples, how the higher judiciary has approached these questions.

static.topic: India–Israel Relations and West Asia Policy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral relations; West Asia
static.whatIsIt: India’s diplomatic, defence, trade and agricultural-technology ties with Israel, balanced against its historical support for Palestinian statehood and a two-state solution.
static.background: India recognised Israel in 1950 but established full diplomatic relations only in 1992. Ties expanded in defence, agriculture and technology, while India continued to voice support for Palestine and a two-state solution. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s 2017 visit to Israel marked a symbolic shift; India has since managed a dehyphenated approach. static.topic: Social Media Content Moderation and Intermediary Liability
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Fundamental rights; regulation of digital platforms
static.whatIsIt: Legal and policy framework under which platforms such as Meta/Instagram moderate user content, claim conditional ‘safe harbour’ and must follow grievance-redressal and transparency obligations under Indian law.
static.background: The IT Act, 2000 provides conditional safe harbour to intermediaries under Section 79. The IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 require grievance officers, compliance reports and timelines for content removal. Courts have examined free-speech limits; Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) struck down Section 66A of the IT Act. Allegations of ‘auto-blocking’ political posts raise questions of due process and transparency.
static.socioEconomic: Political speech, electoral competition, platform accountability and chilling effects on citizens; content moderation decisions affect public discourse at scale.
static.whyInNews: Youth Congress moved Delhi HC alleging Instagram auto-blocked Rahul Gandhi’s posts; Meta met Congress leaders after protests over alleged bias.
static.wayForward: Platforms should publish clear, appealable moderation standards and transparency reports; regulators should ensure due process and free-speech safeguards without creating over-compliance or censorship.
prelimsPointers: Section 79 of the IT Act gives conditional safe harbour to intermediaries.
The IT Rules, 2021 require intermediaries to appoint a grievance officer and publish compliance reports.
Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) struck down Section 66A of the IT Act.

stories.headline: IBM ends US visa sponsorship; Indian H-1B workers get three weeks to exit
stories.summary: IBM has told its US-based H-1B employees that it will no longer sponsor their visas, giving them roughly three weeks to either move into a role outside the United States or leave the company. The decision affects hundreds of Indian professionals and their families, who must choose between relocating — reportedly at a steep cut in pay — and losing both the job and the legal right to remain in the US. The move is being read as part of a wider shift by global technology firms towards local hiring and offshore delivery, and it lands on the community that is the single largest beneficiary of the H-1B programme. For India, the immediate concern is the welfare of affected workers and their dependents; the larger question is the reliability of the US as a destination for skilled Indian talent.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly links immigration policy in a destination country to India's services exports, diaspora welfare and remittance flows — a recurring GS-II and GS-III theme. It also illustrates how employer-tied work visas convert a corporate HR decision into an immigration and livelihood crisis.

perspectives.take: Frames the story through cost and compensation — relocating employees reportedly face a pay cut of up to 80%, spotlighting the wage arbitrage that underpins the offshore delivery model.
Leads on the three-week ultimatum and the procedural vulnerability of H-1B status, foregrounding the legal precarity of visa-tied employment.
Emphasises scale and domestic impact — hundreds of Indians facing exit — treating it as a concern about Indian talent abroad rather than only a corporate story.
Reports from a Gulf and wider diaspora vantage point, framing Indian tech workers as caught 'in a bind' between relocation and job loss, with an eye on mobility across all destination markets.

static.topic: H-1B Visa Programme and India–US Talent Mobility
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral Relations: India and the United States; Effect of policies of developed countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: The H-1B is a US non-immigrant, employer-sponsored work visa for 'specialty occupations' requiring at least a bachelor's degree or its equivalent. It is the principal route for Indian IT professionals to work in the US, permits dual intent (temporary work alongside pursuit of permanent residency), and is subject to an annual numerical cap.
static.background: Created under the Immigration Act of 1990, the H-1B cap was set at 65,000, with a further 20,000 reserved for holders of US master's degrees or higher. Indian nationals have consistently been the largest beneficiary group. Periodic tightening — higher fees, stricter site visits, the 2017 'Buy American, Hire American' executive order and the 2020 suspension of new H-1B entries — has made the route more uncertain. Per-country green card caps under the Immigration and Nationality Act create multi-decade backlogs for Indian applicants.
static.geography: United States; Indian professionals are concentrated in California's Bay Area, Texas, New Jersey and Washington state.
static.socioEconomic: The visa is tied to a specific sponsoring employer, so the end of sponsorship can mean loss of legal status within a short window, simultaneously affecting spouses and children on dependent visas. Indian IT services firms depend on it for onsite delivery, while the US technology sector depends on it for talent.
static.whyInNews: IBM has ended US visa sponsorship, giving its H-1B employees a short window to relocate or leave the company.
static.wayForward: India's long-pending demand for a Totalization Agreement on social security, stronger mobility provisions in bilateral trade and immigration dialogues, and a decisive shift by Indian firms towards local hiring, nearshore centres and remote delivery are the practical responses.
prelimsPointers: H-1B cap: 65,000 general plus 20,000 for holders of US advanced degrees; certain non-profit and research institutions are exempt.
H-1B is employer-specific and job-specific; H-4 is the dependent visa for spouses and children.
India is the largest recipient of H-1B visas among all countries.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how restrictive turns in US immigration policy affect India's services exports, its diaspora and the wider bilateral relationship, and evaluate India's options.

static.topic: Indian Diaspora and Remittances
static.syllabusNode: Indian Society — Role of the Diaspora; Population and Associated Issues
static.whatIsIt: The Indian diaspora — NRIs and Persons of Indian Origin — numbers over 30 million and is spread across the Gulf, North America, Europe, Southeast Asia, Africa and the Caribbean. It is a major source of remittances, investment and soft power.
static.background: Nineteenth-century indentured and 'kangani' migration to Mauritius, Fiji, the Caribbean and Southeast Asia was followed by post-1947 professional migration to the UK, US and Canada, and by 1970s–80s oil-boom migration to the Gulf. Diaspora policy is anchored in the Ministry of External Affairs, Pravasi Bharatiya Divas and the Pravasi Bharatiya Samman, with the OCI scheme providing a long-term visa-free travel facility.
static.geography: Gulf (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman), North America (US, Canada), UK, Southeast Asia (Malaysia, Singapore), Mauritius, Fiji and the Caribbean.
static.socioEconomic: India is the world's largest recipient of international remittances, which have at times exceeded combined FDI inflows and support household consumption, education and health spending, notably in Kerala, Gujarat, Punjab, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh. Skilled migration also raises 'brain drain' concerns, increasingly offset by return migration and 'brain gain'.
static.whyInNews: The IBM visa decision affects Indian professionals in the US, a high-value segment of the diaspora, with possible knock-on effects on mobility and remittance patterns.
static.wayForward: Deepen diaspora engagement, negotiate social security agreements, ease return migration and portability of skills, and diversify migration destinations beyond a few markets.
prelimsPointers: India is the world's largest recipient of international remittances.
OCI cardholders are foreign nationals of Indian origin and do not enjoy voting rights in India.
Pravasi Bharatiya Divas is observed on 9 January.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the contribution of the Indian diaspora to India's economy and external relations, and the challenges posed by restrictive immigration regimes in destination countries.

static.topic: India's IT–BPM Services Exports and the Onsite–Offshore Model
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Changes in Industrial Policy and their Effects on Industrial Growth; Services Sector
static.whatIsIt: India's IT and business services sector is a leading export earner, built on a global delivery model that combines offshore delivery centres in India with onsite staff stationed at client locations abroad.
static.background: The sector expanded from the 1990s on the back of liberalisation, the Y2K transition and the offshore-outsourcing boom. Visa restrictions in the 2000s and 2010s pushed firms to increase local hiring in the US and to move up the value chain into digital, cloud and AI services.
static.geography: Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Noida and Gurugram are the principal delivery hubs.
static.socioEconomic: The sector is a major formal employer and a critical source of foreign exchange; onsite visa costs and restrictions directly affect margins and the ability to win and retain clients.
static.whyInNews: IBM's decision to stop US visa sponsorship signals a wider industry shift towards local hiring and offshoring in global technology services.
static.wayForward: Increase local hiring and nearshore centres, invest in higher-value digital and AI services, and negotiate mobility provisions in bilateral trade agreements.
prelimsPointers: Software and business services are among India's largest services export categories.
GATS Mode 4 refers to the movement of natural persons for the supply of services.
Services exports act as a key cushion against India's merchandise trade deficit.
static.mainsAngle: Analyse how immigration restrictions in major markets affect India's IT services exports and discuss the strategies firms and the government can adopt in response.

prelims: H-1B is a US non-immigrant work visa for specialty occupations, capped at 65,000 annually plus 20,000 for holders of US advanced degrees.
H-1B is employer-specific: if sponsorship ends, the worker's legal status is at risk unless a new sponsor is found or status is changed.
H-4 is the dependent visa for spouses and children of H-1B holders.
India is the largest recipient of H-1B visas and the world's largest recipient of international remittances.
stories.mainsQuestion: The mobility of skilled professionals is central to India's services exports and diaspora linkages. In the light of recent decisions by major global technology employers to withdraw US work-visa sponsorship, examine the implications for India's economy and outline a strategy for the government and industry.

stories.headline: Gaza strike kills deputy education minister as Israeli coalition talks advance
stories.summary: An Israeli airstrike hit an apartment in Deir Al-Balah in the central Gaza Strip, killing Khaled Abu Nada, the Hamas-appointed Deputy Education Minister for Gaza, and his wife, along with others; medics and officials put the overall death toll at nine, while some wire reports said ten. Hamas said it was weighing its response to the killings. In parallel, coalition negotiations in Israel advanced as Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party reached an agreement with the left-leaning Democrats, following a similar deal with the right-wing Israel Beiteinu party on November 24. Together the two developments point to a volatile mix of continuing military operations in Gaza and a fluid political realignment inside Israel.
stories.whyItMatters: West Asia is central to India's energy, diaspora, defence and connectivity interests, and the trajectory of the Gaza conflict together with Israel's coalition arithmetic shapes the regional environment in which India's de-hyphenated ties with Israel and Palestine operate. The coalition-building process also offers a comparative politics case study of proportional-representation government formation.

perspectives.take: Frames the coalition deal as evidence that talks are 'gaining steam' while separately stressing that Hamas is weighing a response to the Gaza killings — emphasis on political process plus escalation risk.
Saudi-based pan-Arab outlet foregrounds the Palestinian casualty toll and Hamas's deliberations, reflecting the priorities of a regional Arab audience.

static.topic: India–Israel Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral, Regional and Global Groupings; India and its Neighbourhood-plus (West Asia)
static.whatIsIt: India's diplomatic, defence, agricultural and technological partnership with Israel, maintained alongside India's longstanding political support for Palestinian statehood.
static.background: India recognised Israel in 1950 but avoided full diplomatic ties for decades while backing the Palestinian cause; full diplomatic relations were established in 1992. Defence procurement and agricultural technology became major pillars from the late 1990s onwards. India's approach is commonly described as 'de-hyphenation' — engaging Israel and Palestine on separate tracks. India is also a member of the I2U2 grouping with Israel, the UAE and the United States.
static.geography: West Asia/Levant; Israel borders Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Egypt and the Mediterranean Sea.
static.socioEconomic: Trade spans diamonds, chemicals and machinery; Israeli drip-irrigation and desalination technologies are used in Indian agriculture, and labour-mobility arrangements for Indian workers in Israel's construction and caregiving sectors have been discussed and signed in recent years.
static.whyInNews: Continuing Israeli military operations in Gaza and a fluid coalition realignment inside Israel shape the political environment in which India–Israel and India–Palestine ties are conducted.
static.wayForward: Maintain the de-hyphenation balance — sustaining the strategic and technological partnership with Israel while upholding India's stated support for a two-state solution and for international humanitarian law.

India is a founding member of I2U2 along with Israel, the UAE and the United States.
India's stated position supports a sovereign, independent and viable Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital.
