static.topic: Israel–Palestine Conflict and International Humanitarian Law
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — West Asia; International Law and Humanitarian Law
static.whatIsIt: The long-running Israeli–Palestinian conflict, currently centred on Gaza, governed in conduct by IHL principles of distinction, proportionality and protection of civilians, including humanitarian and medical personnel.
static.background: Rooted in competing national claims over the same territory, the conflict runs through the 1947 UN partition plan, the wars of 1948, 1967 and 1973, the Oslo Accords of 1993, the second Intifada, Israel's 2005 disengagement from Gaza, Hamas's assumption of control in Gaza in 2007 and the subsequent blockade, and the war that began in October 2023 followed by repeated ceasefire and negotiation cycles mediated by Qatar, Egypt and the United States.
static.geography: The Gaza Strip is a small, densely populated Mediterranean coastal territory bordering Israel and Egypt, with the Rafah crossing on the Egyptian border.
static.socioEconomic: The population is heavily dependent on humanitarian assistance, including UNRWA education and health services, with restricted movement of people and goods and very high unemployment.
static.whyInNews: An Israeli strike in Deir Al-Balah killed the Hamas-appointed Deputy Education Minister for Gaza and others, and Hamas said it was weighing its response.
static.wayForward: A durable ceasefire, unimpeded humanitarian access and revival of a credible political process aimed at a two-state solution remain the widely advocated path.
prelimsPointers: UNRWA was created by the UN General Assembly in 1949 to assist Palestinian refugees.
The Gaza Strip borders Israel and Egypt; the Rafah crossing lies on the Egypt border.
The Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their Additional Protocols form the core of international humanitarian law.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the relevance and limits of international humanitarian law in contemporary asymmetric conflicts, with reference to Gaza.

static.topic: Coalition Politics and Government Formation in Israel
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Comparison of the Indian constitutional scheme with that of other countries
static.whatIsIt: Israel's parliamentary system, in which a 120-member Knesset is elected by proportional representation from a single nationwide constituency and governments are formed by multi-party coalitions.
static.background: Israel has no single written constitution and is governed instead by Basic Laws. The Knesset has 120 members, so a coalition needs 61 seats for a majority, making coalitions the norm; an electoral threshold, raised to 3.25% in 2014, applies. The President consults parties and invites a member to form a government. Five Knesset elections were held between 2019 and 2022, illustrating the fragmentation of the party system.
static.socioEconomic: Proportional representation gives small parties outsized leverage, and coalition agreements typically distribute ministries, budgets and policy commitments among partners.
static.whyInNews: Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party reached a coalition agreement with the left-leaning Democrats, after a similar deal with the right-wing Israel Beiteinu party on November 24.
prelimsPointers: The Knesset has 120 members; 61 seats are needed for a majority.
Israel has no single written constitution; Basic Laws perform that function.
The Knesset electoral threshold is 3.25%.
static.mainsAngle: Compare coalition government formation in Israel and India, and assess the implications of fragmented legislatures for governance stability.

prelims: Israel's Knesset has 120 members; a coalition requires 61 seats and the electoral threshold is 3.25%.
Israel has no single written constitution and is governed through Basic Laws.
India recognised Israel in 1950 and established full diplomatic relations in 1992; it supports a two-state solution.
UNRWA, set up by the UN General Assembly in 1949, delivers education, health and relief services to Palestinian refugees.
stories.mainsQuestion: The continuing conflict in Gaza and Israel's coalition realignment are together reshaping West Asia's political map. Examine the implications for India's de-hyphenation policy and its wider West Asia strategy.

stories.headline: RBI lines up ₹75,000 crore VRR auction; Supreme Court presses bank chiefs on sanctions
stories.summary: The Reserve Bank of India has announced a 3-day Variable Rate Repo (VRR) auction under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility for Friday, 27 November 2026, with a notified amount of ₹75,000 crore, a 09:30–10:00 AM window and reversal on Monday, 30 November 2026. The RBI described the move as a response to a review of current and evolving near-term liquidity conditions, making it a routine but sizeable injection of durable short-term funds into the banking system. Separately, the Supreme Court, hearing a builder–bank nexus matter, directed the chiefs of HDFC and ICICI Bank to grant the required prosecution sanctions or appear before the court in person. Together the two developments frame the day's banking story: the central bank managing system liquidity on one side, and the judiciary asserting accountability over bank decision-making on the other.
stories.whyItMatters: The VRR auction illustrates how the RBI uses LAF tools beyond the policy repo rate to manage liquidity, a recurring Prelims and Mains theme in monetary policy. The Supreme Court's direction tests the boundary between statutory sanction requirements for prosecution and judicial oversight of bank chiefs, a live GS-II judiciary question.

perspectives.take: Frames the VRR auction as a technical, routine liquidity-management operation triggered by an assessment of evolving near-term liquidity conditions — neutral, official and non-political in tone.
Legal-reporting framing that foregrounds judicial pressure on private bank leadership in a builder–bank nexus case, emphasising accountability and the court's willingness to summon top executives.

static.topic: Reserve Bank of India & Monetary Policy
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking & Monetary Policy; RBI functions and liquidity management
static.whatIsIt: The RBI, India's central bank, conducts monetary policy through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (2016) with a 4% CPI inflation target (±2%). The Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) is its operating framework for managing day-to-day liquidity using repo and reverse repo operations, including Variable Rate Repo (VRR) auctions where the rate is discovered through bidding rather than fixed.
static.background: Established in 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934 and nationalised in 1949. The inflation-targeting MPC framework followed the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) and a 2016 amendment to the RBI Act. VRR auctions are used when the RBI wants to inject liquidity at a market-determined rate, typically alongside or instead of fixed-rate repo operations.
static.socioEconomic: Liquidity conditions affect banks' cost of funds and hence lending rates transmitted to borrowers through MCLR and EBLR; tight liquidity can push up short-term rates even without a repo change.
static.whyInNews: The RBI announced a 3-day VRR auction of ₹75,000 crore on 27 November 2026, with reversal on 30 November 2026, citing evolving near-term liquidity conditions.
static.wayForward: Improve liquidity forecasting and communication so that VRR/LAF operations are read as signals rather than surprises; strengthen monetary transmission so liquidity operations reach borrowers.
prelimsPointers: Repo is the rate at which RBI lends to banks against securities; reverse repo is the absorbing rate.
MPC has 6 members — 3 from RBI (Governor as chair) and 3 external; the Governor has a casting vote.
Inflation target: 4% CPI with a 2–6% band, reviewed every five years.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the RBI's LAF operations, including VRR auctions, complement the policy repo rate in managing liquidity, and assess the effectiveness of monetary transmission to borrowers.

static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts & Judicial Review
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary; judicial review, judicial activism and accountability of economic actors
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution, exercising judicial review and writ jurisdiction under Article 32. Courts can direct statutory authorities and, in appropriate cases, require compliance or personal appearance of senior executives.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine; PILs from the late 1970s expanded access to justice. Statutory provisions generally require prior sanction before prosecuting certain officials, and courts have repeatedly ruled on delays in deciding such sanction requests.
static.socioEconomic: Bank–builder linkages and delays in sanctioning prosecution raise questions about governance standards in lending and the credibility of regulatory and audit oversight in the financial sector.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court directed the chiefs of HDFC and ICICI Bank to grant prosecution sanctions in a builder–bank nexus matter or appear before the court.
static.wayForward: Set clear timelines for deciding prosecution sanction requests, strengthen bank boards and audit committees on related-party and builder exposures, and preserve the balance between judicial oversight and institutional autonomy.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction over Centre–state disputes lies with the Supreme Court under Article 131.
Advisory jurisdiction is under Article 143.
Article 32 provides writ jurisdiction to the Supreme Court; Article 226 to High Courts.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the balance between judicial independence and accountability, and examine whether judicial directions to grant prosecution sanctions strengthen or unsettle statutory decision-making processes.

The Supreme Court directed the HDFC and ICICI Bank chiefs to grant prosecution sanctions in a builder–bank nexus case or appear before it.
The MPC, instituted in 2016, has six members and an inflation target of 4% CPI within a 2–6% band.
stories.mainsQuestion: The RBI's liquidity operations and the judiciary's scrutiny of bank decision-making both shape the credibility of India's financial system. Critically examine how monetary policy tools and judicial accountability mechanisms complement each other in strengthening banking governance.

stories.headline: Kerala's coast erodes: homes, livelihoods and freshwater at risk
stories.summary: Relentless shoreline erosion along Kerala's coast is pushing families in vulnerable villages such as Pozhiyoor to the edge, with existing seawalls proving inadequate against advancing waves. Homes, fishing-based livelihoods and freshwater reserves are all under strain as seawater advances and saline intrusion reaches wells and coastal aquifers. The state's relocation and rehabilitation efforts provide only temporary relief, as resettlement is often partial, distant from livelihoods and unsupported by secure tenure. The story links a slow-onset physical process — shoreline retreat — to a human crisis of displacement, making coastal erosion as much a governance and social-protection problem as an environmental one.
stories.whyItMatters: Coastal erosion is a slow-onset disaster that UPSC links to CRZ regulation, disaster management and climate-induced displacement — an emerging area of both GS-I geography and GS-III environment questions.

perspectives.take: Frames erosion through the lived experience of coastal communities — failing seawalls, threatened freshwater and inadequate relocation — reflecting an environment-and-development, community-rights lens rather than a purely technical one.

static.topic: Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) and Coastal Zone Management
static.syllabusNode: Environment & Ecology — Environmental legislation and coastal regulation
static.whatIsIt: The CRZ regime regulates permissible activities along India's coast through a notification issued under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. It classifies the coast into CRZ-I (ecologically sensitive), CRZ-II (developed), CRZ-III (rural) and CRZ-IV (water area up to 12 nautical miles), and mandates Coastal Zone Management Plans prepared by States and approved through the national and state coastal zone management authorities.
static.background: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 was enacted invoking Article 253 to give effect to decisions of the Stockholm Conference, and the first CRZ Notification followed in 1991. It was revised in 2011 and replaced by the CRZ Notification, 2019, which introduced sub-categories such as CRZ-IIIA and IIIB with differentiated No Development Zones based on population density, and eased norms for certain activities. Scientific support comes from the National Centre for Sustainable Coastal Management (NCSCM), Chennai, while shoreline-change assessment is carried out by the National Centre for Coastal Research (NCCR) under the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
static.geography: India's coastline runs over 7,500 km including islands, spanning nine coastal states and four Union Territories. Kerala's coast is about 590 km long, spread across nine coastal districts, and is heavily built up with seawalls and dense coastal settlements.
static.socioEconomic: Coastal Kerala is densely populated, with fishing, tourism, coir and allied activities sustaining lakhs of households. Erosion and saline intrusion damage homes, fishing infrastructure and drinking-water sources, and resettlement often distances communities from their livelihood base, aggravating vulnerability.
static.whyInNews: Reports from Kerala's coastal villages describe advancing shorelines, ineffective seawalls and the strain on freshwater reserves, with state relocation efforts offering only temporary relief.
static.wayForward: Strengthen shoreline monitoring and sediment-cell-based management, prioritise soft and hybrid protection measures over seawalls where feasible, integrate erosion risk into coastal land-use and building plans, and design relocation packages that are voluntary, tenure-secure and linked to livelihood restoration.
prelimsPointers: CRZ categories: CRZ-I (ecologically sensitive), CRZ-II (developed), CRZ-III (rural), CRZ-IV (water area up to 12 nautical miles).
The CRZ Notification is issued under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, which itself was enacted using Article 253.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether India's CRZ framework, largely a regulatory no-development model, adequately addresses shoreline erosion and the displacement it causes.

static.topic: Coastal erosion, saline intrusion and climate-induced displacement
static.syllabusNode: Disaster Management — Slow-onset disasters and climate adaptation; GS-I Geography — Coastal landforms and processes
static.whatIsIt: Coastal erosion is the net loss of land along the shore due to wave action, currents, sediment deficit and sea-level rise, compounded by hard structures, sand mining and port and harbour development. It is classified as a slow-onset hazard, and its effects include loss of land and property, saline intrusion into aquifers, and distress migration.
static.background: National shoreline-change assessments by the NCCR, using multi-decadal satellite data, indicate that roughly a third of India's coastline is eroding, with a smaller share accreting and the rest stable. Kerala has a long history of seawall construction as its principal erosion-control response, but seawalls can shift erosion to adjacent stretches and do not address the underlying sediment deficit or sea-level rise. India's disaster framework under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 has traditionally focused on sudden-onset events such as cyclones, floods and tsunamis.
static.geography: Erosion hotspots occur along the Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Odisha and West Bengal coasts, with the problem sharpest near river mouths and in stretches where natural sediment supply has been interrupted.
static.socioEconomic: Displacement is typically distress-driven and unplanned. Fishing households lose access to beaches used for boat parking, net drying and fish landing, while women and the elderly face heightened health and water-security burdens. Saline intrusion raises the cost of drinking water and can render coastal agriculture unviable.
static.whyInNews: Kerala's coastal communities are reported to be losing land, homes and freshwater sources, with relocation offering only short-term relief.
static.wayForward: Move from a purely structural response to integrated coastal zone management — beach nourishment, dune and mangrove restoration, sediment budgeting, setback lines enforced in practice, and a formal policy on climate-induced displacement with livelihood-linked, community-consented resettlement.
prelimsPointers: NCCR's shoreline change assessment, based on satellite data, indicates roughly one-third of India's coastline is under erosion.
Seawalls are hard protection structures; they can transfer erosion to adjoining stretches rather than eliminate it.
static.mainsAngle: Coastal erosion is a slow-onset disaster with acute consequences. Discuss the adequacy of India's coastal protection and disaster management frameworks in dealing with erosion-induced displacement.

static.topic: Coastal regulation and Centre–State relations
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union: powers are divided between the Union and States via the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule), with residuary powers with the Union (Art. 248).
static.background: Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) Commissions examined Centre-State balance. The Governor (Art. 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a flashpoint over assent to Bills (Art. 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Art. 201).
static.geography: Coastal regulation operates on this federal terrain: the Union sets the CRZ framework under a central law, while States and Union Territories prepare and implement Coastal Zone Management Plans through their state coastal zone management authorities.
static.socioEconomic: States with dense coastal settlements and livelihood-dependent populations frequently seek relaxations for fishing harbours, ports, roads and housing, setting up a recurring tension between conservation mandates and local development demands.
static.whyInNews: Erosion-driven distress in Kerala highlights how central coastal regulation and state-level implementation and rehabilitation responsibilities intersect in practice.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise structured Centre-State consultation on coastal management, with clear cost-sharing for protection works and resettlement, and predictable, time-bound approvals rather than case-by-case relaxations.
prelimsPointers: Concurrent List: union law prevails on repugnancy unless state law reserved for President's assent (Art. 254).
Inter-State Council (Art. 263) is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.
static.mainsAngle: Recent spats over Governor's assent and fiscal devolution — assess cooperative federalism in practice, using environmental regulation and coastal management as examples.

prelims: The CRZ Notification, issued under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, classifies the coast into CRZ-I, II, III and IV, with CRZ-IV covering the water area up to 12 nautical miles.
Kerala's coastline is about 590 km long and spans nine coastal districts; India's total coastline, including islands, exceeds 7,500 km.

The National Centre for Coastal Research (NCCR, Ministry of Earth Sciences) carries out national shoreline-change assessment; the National Centre for Sustainable Coastal Management (NCSCM) supports coastal zone mapping and management.
Coastal erosion is a slow-onset hazard, whereas India's disaster management framework has historically prioritised sudden-onset events such as cyclones, floods and tsunamis.
stories.mainsQuestion: Coastal erosion is often described as a slow-onset disaster with acute social consequences. Examine the adequacy of India's coastal regulation and disaster management framework in addressing erosion-induced displacement, with reference to Kerala.

stories.headline: Private rocket firm sets sights on daily launches from India
stories.summary: The Indian Express profiles the private launch company that carried out India's first privately developed rocket mission, reporting that the firm now aims for a launch-a-day cadence. The report traces the company's forward roadmap — scaling up launch frequency, developing larger orbital vehicles and building a customer base in the small-satellite market. It situates this ambition within India's opening of the space sector to private players through IN-SPACe and NSIL, and the wider push to grow the domestic space economy. The account is largely industry-facing, focusing on manufacturing capacity, funding and the regulatory pathway rather than on government policy itself.
stories.whyItMatters: Private launch capability is central to India's bid to capture a share of the global small-satellite launch market and to GS-III questions on space commercialisation, IN-SPACe/NSIL and space governance.

perspectives.take: Frames the story as an industry-ambition and business-roadmap piece — a city-page report on one firm's growth plans, launch cadence and commercial prospects, with limited scrutiny of regulatory or strategic constraints.

articles.title: ‘A launch every day our goal’: What lies ahead for firm that sent India’s first private rocket into space

static.topic: India's Space Programme (ISRO)
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Space
static.whatIsIt: ISRO, set up in 1969, runs India's space programme for communication, remote sensing, navigation (NavIC) and exploration, under the Department of Space. IN-SPACe (announced 2020) and NSIL now promote private participation alongside the state programme.
static.background: Aryabhata (1975) was India's first satellite. Mangalyaan (2013) reached Mars orbit on its first attempt. Chandrayaan-3 soft-landed near the lunar south pole in 2023. Gaganyaan is India's first crewed mission. The sector was opened to private entities through IN-SPACe and NSIL, with a national space policy framework following.
static.geography: Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota (Andhra Pradesh) is the principal launch site; Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, Thumba (Kerala); ISRO headquarters in Bengaluru.
static.socioEconomic: Space applications support agriculture, disaster management, telemedicine, tele-education and navigation; the commercial space economy is a growing source of high-skill employment and startup activity.
static.whyInNews: A private Indian firm that conducted the country's first privately developed rocket launch has outlined an ambition of near-daily launch operations.
static.wayForward: Scale domestic launch capacity while strengthening space-debris mitigation, insurance and liability frameworks, and deepening the private–ISRO partnership.
prelimsPointers: PSLV is India's workhorse launcher; GSLV Mk-III can carry heavier geosynchronous payloads.
India is a founder of the Outer Space Treaty framework; UN COPUOS governs space law.
static.mainsAngle: Commercialisation of space, space debris and India's role in space governance.

static.topic: Private Participation in India's Space Sector
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Space; Economy — Industrial Policy
static.whatIsIt: A reform architecture that lets private companies build satellites and launch vehicles, own and operate ground stations, and offer space-based services, with IN-SPACe as the single-window regulator/promoter and NSIL as the state's commercial arm.
static.background: IN-SPACe was announced in 2020 to handhold and authorise private space activity; NSIL was created as a public-sector enterprise to commercially exploit ISRO's capabilities. India's first privately developed rocket was launched in 2022, marking the entry of private launch vehicles. A national space policy subsequently set out roles for ISRO, IN-SPACe, NSIL and private actors.
static.socioEconomic: Aims to grow India's share of the global space economy, attract foreign and domestic investment, and create a startup ecosystem around small-satellite launch and applications.
static.whyInNews: A private launch firm's stated goal of a launch every day illustrates how far private launch ambitions have moved beyond a single demonstration flight.
static.wayForward: Clear, predictable licensing timelines; a dedicated space-activity law covering liability, insurance and debris; assured demand through government anchor contracts; and technology-transfer mechanisms from ISRO.
prelimsPointers: IN-SPACe functions as the single-window autonomous agency for private space activities; NSIL is the commercial arm under the Department of Space.
Private participation spans satellite manufacturing, launch vehicles, ground-segment services and space-based applications.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India's institutional framework for private space activity is adequate to convert startup ambition into a durable commercial launch industry.

prelims: ISRO was established in 1969; IN-SPACe (announced 2020) is the single-window agency for private space activities and NSIL is the state's commercial arm.
India's first privately developed rocket launch took place in 2022, opening the private launch-vehicle segment in the country.
PSLV is India's workhorse launch vehicle, while GSLV Mk-III is designed for heavier geosynchronous payloads.
UN COPUOS is the principal multilateral forum for space law; India is a founder of the Outer Space Treaty framework.
stories.mainsQuestion: India's private space sector has moved from a single demonstration launch to ambitions of high-frequency commercial operations. Examine the role of IN-SPACe and NSIL in enabling this transition, and identify the regulatory, financial and strategic constraints that must be addressed for India to become a competitive launch hub.

stories.headline: TB returns in cured patients, spotlight on relapse care gap
stories.summary: Doctors in Delhi are reporting a steady stream of patients who were declared cured after a full course of tuberculosis treatment but have fallen ill with TB again, pointing to a poorly tracked problem of relapse and reinfection. Clinicians attribute the pattern to a mix of incomplete or interrupted therapy, undetected drug resistance, malnutrition and other co-morbidities, and residual lung damage that leaves patients vulnerable to a second episode. Because India's TB programme is largely organised around detecting and completing treatment, post-treatment surveillance and follow-up care remain thin, so recurrences often surface late. The trend complicates the country's stated goal of eliminating TB by 2025 and raises questions about how 'cure' is defined and verified. It also shifts attention to the social determinants — nutrition, housing, income loss — that drive both initial infection and recurrence.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly relevant to GS-II health governance and welfare delivery, and to GS-III questions on antimicrobial resistance and disease surveillance; TB relapse and drug resistance are recurring themes in UPSC prelims and in mains answers on India's public health architecture and SDG-3 commitments.

perspectives.take: Frames the issue through patient and clinician accounts in Delhi, emphasising that 'cured' patients returning with TB exposes gaps in post-treatment follow-up rather than a failure of first-line drugs alone; a national daily with an urban health-systems lens.

articles.title: Treated, cured, then sick again: Why tuberculosis keeps returning to haunt patients

static.topic: National TB Elimination Programme and post-treatment relapse
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Health, Government Policies and Interventions
static.whatIsIt: India's flagship public-health programme for tuberculosis, providing free diagnosis, free anti-TB drugs, treatment adherence support and notification through the Nikshay digital portal. It defines treatment success through microbiological and clinical criteria, but has limited structured mechanisms for long-term follow-up of patients after they are declared cured.
static.background: A National TB Programme existed from 1962; it was revamped as the Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) in 1997 with the DOTS strategy of directly observed short-course treatment. Tuberculosis was made a notifiable disease in 2012. The programme was renamed the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) in 2020, and the government adopted a National Strategic Plan built on the pillars of Detect, Treat, Prevent and Build, with a stated target of TB elimination in India by 2025, ahead of the global SDG timeline of 2030.
static.geography: India-wide, with the burden concentrated in populous northern and western states and in dense urban settlements such as Delhi, where overcrowding and poor ventilation aid transmission.
static.socioEconomic: TB is strongly associated with poverty, undernutrition, poor housing, indoor air pollution, diabetes and stigma. Catastrophic out-of-pocket costs push affected households further into distress, and nutritional support is a recognised part of treatment success.
static.whyInNews: Reports of patients in Delhi being declared cured and then falling ill with tuberculosis again have drawn attention to relapse, reinfection and post-TB lung disease, and to the absence of routine post-treatment surveillance.
static.wayForward: Strengthen post-treatment follow-up and active surveillance after 'cure', use universal drug-susceptibility testing to catch resistance early, expand nutritional and social support, integrate TB care with diabetes and HIV services, and invest in airborne infection control in crowded settings.
prelimsPointers: Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and spreads through airborne droplets; it was made a notifiable disease in India in 2012.
RNTCP (1997) was renamed the National TB Elimination Programme in 2020; India's stated elimination target is 2025, ahead of the SDG target year of 2030.
Nikshay is the government's web-based TB notification and patient-tracking portal.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why treatment 'cure' in tuberculosis does not guarantee freedom from disease, and suggest programme reforms needed for post-treatment surveillance in India.

static.topic: Welfare delivery and nutritional support for TB patients
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare Schemes and Rights-based Entitlements
static.whatIsIt: India's welfare model combines rights-based legislation with direct benefit transfer (DBT) routed through the Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile (JAM) backbone. For TB patients this includes cash nutritional support under the Nikshay Poshan Yojana and health-financing cover through the Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY insurance arm.
static.background: Rights-based laws such as MGNREGA (2005), the Right to Education (2009) and the National Food Security Act (2013) were followed by DBT-linked schemes. Ayushman Bharat (2018) has an insurance component (PM-JAY) and a network of Health and Wellness Centres. POSHAN Abhiyaan addresses malnutrition, a major driver of TB risk.
static.socioEconomic: Nutritional support and financial protection reduce treatment interruption and relapse risk; exclusion errors in beneficiary lists, urban poverty and informal employment remain barriers to reaching all TB-affected households.
static.whyInNews: Recurrence of TB in cured patients renews focus on whether nutritional and income support reaches patients for the full duration of treatment and recovery.
static.wayForward: Reduce exclusion errors in DBT and ration entitlements, extend nutritional support beyond the treatment period where clinically indicated, and link TB patients to wider social-security and employment support.
prelimsPointers: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year.
Four labour codes consolidate 29 existing labour laws.
Ayushman Bharat (2018) has a health-insurance arm (PM-JAY) and a primary-care component of Health and Wellness Centres.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how nutritional and income-support interventions can improve tuberculosis treatment outcomes, and assess the limitations of DBT-based welfare delivery for marginalised patients.

static.topic: Drug-resistant TB and antimicrobial resistance
static.syllabusNode: Science and Technology — Health, Biotechnology and Antimicrobial Resistance
static.whatIsIt: Drug-resistant tuberculosis arises when Mycobacterium tuberculosis develops resistance to first-line drugs, producing multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) forms that require longer, more toxic and costlier regimens. It is a key component of the wider global antimicrobial resistance crisis.
static.background: Resistance is driven by incomplete or irregular treatment, poor drug quality, transmission of already-resistant strains and diagnostic delay. WHO's End TB Strategy, aligned with SDG target 3.3, sets milestones for reducing TB incidence and deaths by 2030. Newer drugs and shorter oral regimens have improved outcomes but access and monitoring remain uneven.
static.geography: A global problem with the highest absolute burden in South and Southeast Asia, including India.
static.socioEconomic: Resistant TB imposes far higher treatment costs, longer work absence and greater stigma, deepening household financial hardship.
static.whyInNews: Recurrent disease in previously treated patients is one of the routes through which drug-resistant TB is detected, making relapse surveillance central to resistance control.
static.wayForward: Universal drug-susceptibility testing at diagnosis, adherence support, rational antibiotic use under a national action plan on antimicrobial resistance, and surveillance linking treatment records to resistance data.
prelimsPointers: WHO's End TB Strategy is aligned with SDG target 3.3, which aims to end the TB epidemic by 2030.
MDR-TB is resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin, the two most powerful first-line anti-TB drugs.
static.mainsAngle: Analyse how inadequate treatment completion and weak post-treatment surveillance contribute to drug-resistant tuberculosis, and evaluate India's response under its national antimicrobial resistance framework.

prelims: Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and spreads through airborne droplets; India made it a notifiable disease in 2012.
A patient declared cured can still develop TB again through relapse (reactivation of the same infection) or reinfection (a fresh infection), and may also be left with post-TB lung disease.
Incomplete treatment, undetected drug resistance and undernutrition are the principal drivers of recurrence.
India's stated goal is TB elimination by 2025 under the National TB Elimination Programme, ahead of the SDG target of 2030.
stories.mainsQuestion: Recurrence of tuberculosis in patients declared cured exposes the limits of a treatment-centric approach to disease control. Critically examine the gaps in India's TB programme and suggest reforms for post-treatment surveillance and social support.

stories.headline: China tells Japan to stop 'stirring up' South China Sea disputes
stories.summary: China's Defence Ministry publicly urged Japan to stop 'stirring up' disputes in the South China Sea, saying Tokyo should not meddle in a region where it has no sovereignty claim. The statement was a direct response to Japan's announcement earlier in the month that it will supply the Philippines with radars and drones to strengthen Manila's coastal surveillance capabilities. The exchange marks another turn in the deepening Japan–Philippines defence relationship, which Beijing reads as part of a wider Indo-Pacific containment architecture. It also keeps the South China Sea in focus ahead of continued ASEAN–China talks on a code of conduct, with competing maritime claims and freedom-of-navigation concerns unresolved.
stories.whyItMatters: The episode illustrates how extra-regional partnerships — Japan's defence transfers to the Philippines — are reshaping the Indo-Pacific balance and testing UNCLOS-based dispute settlement. For India, it is a live case study in strategic autonomy, multi-alignment and the rules-based maritime order it champions.

perspectives.take: Wire-service account sticks closely to the official Chinese statement and the radar-and-drone announcement, presenting both positions without editorialising.
Indian aggregator syndicates the wire copy with a development-and-governance gloss, adding little original reporting or regional nuance.
Hong Kong Chinese-language outlet carries the Chinese defence ministry's phrasing prominently, reflecting a framing closer to Beijing's official position.
Coverage available at source.

static.topic: South China Sea Dispute and UNCLOS
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Indo-Pacific, Maritime Security and Global Groupings
static.whatIsIt: The South China Sea is a semi-enclosed sea in the western Pacific bordered by China, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei, Indonesia and Taiwan. Several states hold overlapping claims over island groups and reefs — notably the Paracels (Xisha), the Spratlys (Nansha) and Scarborough Shoal — and the maritime zones they generate. UNCLOS provides the legal framework for baselines, territorial seas, exclusive economic zones and continental shelves.
static.background: ASEAN and China signed the non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC) in 2002. In 2009 China submitted a map showing a 'nine-dash line' to the UN, prompting objections. In 2013 the Philippines initiated Annex VII arbitration; the tribunal issued its award in 2016, which China rejects and does not participate in. Negotiations on a binding Code of Conduct (COC) between ASEAN and China remain inconclusive.
static.geography: A strategic maritime corridor linking the Indian and Pacific Oceans, adjacent to the Malacca, Sunda and Lombok chokepoints, through which a very large share of global shipping and trade passes. It holds significant fisheries and potential hydrocarbon resources.
static.socioEconomic: Fisheries support the livelihoods of millions of people in littoral states; the sea is central to shipping, energy exploration and the strategic depth of coastal economies. Competing EEZ claims affect fishing rights, resource extraction and maritime governance.
static.whyInNews: China's Defence Ministry urged Japan to stop 'stirring up' South China Sea disputes, responding to Japan's announcement that it will provide the Philippines with radars and drones for coastal surveillance.
static.wayForward: Conclude an effective, UNCLOS-consistent Code of Conduct; preserve ASEAN unity and centrality; pursue peaceful dispute settlement through arbitration and negotiation; and maintain freedom of navigation and overflight consistent with international law.
prelimsPointers: UNCLOS was adopted in 1982 and entered into force in 1994; India ratified it in 1995.
The 2016 Annex VII tribunal award in Philippines v. China rejected the nine-dash line as a basis for historic rights; China rejects the award.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how extra-regional defence partnerships in the Indo-Pacific affect the prospects for a rules-based resolution of South China Sea disputes.

static.topic: India's Foreign Policy and Strategic Autonomy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World, Bilateral and Multilateral Engagements
static.whatIsIt: India's foreign policy combines strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, and the Neighbourhood First and Act East outlooks. It engages across the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA simultaneously.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954). Post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US. The Indo-Pacific concept and Quad (with US, Japan, Australia) gained salience after 2017.
static.whyInNews: Japan–Philippines defence cooperation and China's response sharpen the Indo-Pacific debate in which India balances Quad engagement with its own ties to Beijing and ASEAN.
static.wayForward: Continue issue-based multi-alignment, deepen ASEAN and Indo-Pacific partnerships, and articulate an Indian vision of a free, open and inclusive Indo-Pacific grounded in international law.
prelimsPointers: India assumed the G20 presidency in 2022–23; the African Union was admitted as a permanent G20 member in 2023.
India and Pakistan joined the SCO in 2017.
static.mainsAngle: Balancing ties with the West, Russia and the Global South; India as a 'Voice of the Global South' and bridging power.

static.topic: United Nations and Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and Multilateral Institutions
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion. Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: Contested maritime disputes such as the South China Sea highlight the limits of multilateral enforcement, since UNCLOS dispute settlement can be resisted by a P5 member.
static.wayForward: Push for UNSC expansion and reform, strengthen UNCLOS-based dispute settlement mechanisms, and build coalitions that uphold a rules-based maritime order.
prelimsPointers: The UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent and 10 elected for two-year terms.
The International Court of Justice sits at The Hague; UN headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim rests on representativeness, its population and contributions; assess obstacles such as veto politics and the Ezulwini Consensus.

prelims: China's Defence Ministry statement was a response to Japan's announcement that it will supply the Philippines with radars and drones for coastal surveillance.
UNCLOS (1982, in force 1994) is the legal framework governing maritime zones; India ratified it in 1995.
The 2016 Annex VII arbitral award in Philippines v. China rejected the nine-dash line; China rejects the award and the tribunal's jurisdiction.
ASEAN and China signed the non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea in 2002; Code of Conduct talks continue.
stories.mainsQuestion: The South China Sea dispute increasingly draws in extra-regional powers. Examine how such involvement affects the prospects for a UNCLOS-based settlement, and assess the implications for India's Indo-Pacific strategy.

stories.headline: Ganga Water Treaty renewal stalls as India-Bangladesh ties remain frozen
stories.summary: With the 1996 India-Bangladesh Ganga Waters Treaty due to lapse in December 2026, its renewal remains stalled amid a broader freeze in bilateral engagement. New Delhi has twice extended invitations to Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, but his apparent reluctance to engage India has kept treaty review off the table. The treaty governs lean-season sharing of Ganga flows at the Farakka Barrage and has no automatic rollover, so a lapse would leave the dry-season allocation without a binding framework. Analysts attribute the impasse to political distance between the two neighbours rather than to any technical dispute over the water-sharing formula.
stories.whyItMatters: The treaty's expiry tests India's neighbourhood diplomacy and the credibility of its transboundary water governance, directly affecting farmers in West Bengal and southwestern Bangladesh. It also sets a precedent for other shared rivers, notably the pending Teesta arrangement.

perspectives.take: Frames the treaty's limbo as a symptom of wider political stasis — Dhaka's perceived disinclination to engage, despite two Indian invitations to PM Tarique Rahman, rather than any technical deadlock over the water-sharing formula.
Reports the same impasse as a straight news development, foregrounding the uncertainty over the treaty's future and the absence of forward movement in India-Bangladesh ties.

static.topic: India-Bangladesh Ganga Waters Treaty, 1996
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood; bilateral treaties and agreements
static.whatIsIt: A 30-year bilateral treaty signed on 12 December 1996 that governs the sharing of lean-season (1 January–31 May) Ganga waters at the Farakka Barrage, guaranteeing Bangladesh a defined minimum share of the flow.
static.background: India built the Farakka Barrage in Murshidabad district, West Bengal, commissioned in 1975, to divert Ganga water into the Hooghly to check siltation and protect Kolkata port. Bangladesh objected to unilateral diversion, leading to the 1977 Agreement (Morarji Desai–Ziaur Rahman), followed by MoUs in 1982, 1985 and 1988. The present treaty was signed on 12 December 1996 by Prime Ministers H.D. Deve Gowda and Sheikh Hasina and runs for 30 years, i.e., to December 2026.
static.geography: The Ganga enters Bangladesh as the Padma; the Farakka Barrage lies in Murshidabad district, West Bengal, close to the Bangladesh border, and is the point at which the treaty's flow measurements are taken.
static.socioEconomic: Lean-season flows sustain irrigation, inland fisheries, navigation and drinking-water supply in southwestern Bangladesh and parts of West Bengal; shortfalls hit rice cultivation and rural livelihoods on both sides.
static.whyInNews: The treaty is due to lapse in December 2026 and its renewal has stalled amid a broader stasis in India-Bangladesh relations.
static.wayForward: Early technical-level talks on a successor framework, joint basin-level data sharing and flow monitoring, and a deliberate effort to delink water cooperation from the wider political cycle.
prelimsPointers: The Ganga Waters Treaty was signed on 12 December 1996 and is valid for 30 years, expiring in December 2026.
Bangladesh is guaranteed 35,000 cusecs when the 10-day average flow at Farakka is 75,000 cusecs or more, with the share tapering in leaner periods.
The treaty allocates only dry-season flows (1 January–31 May); monsoon flows are not shared under it.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how bilateral political trust shapes transboundary water institutions, using the Ganga Waters Treaty as a case study.

static.topic: India-Bangladesh Transboundary River Cooperation
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbours; regional cooperation and river water disputes
static.whatIsIt: The institutional framework through which India and Bangladesh manage their shared rivers, principally the Joint Rivers Commission (1972) and river-specific arrangements such as the 1996 Ganga treaty.
static.background: The Joint Rivers Commission was set up in 1972 to address boundary river issues. The 1996 Ganga treaty remains the only comprehensive water-sharing agreement between the two countries; the Teesta agreement has stayed unsigned since a draft was readied in 2011, largely because of opposition from the West Bengal government. Other shared rivers such as the Feni, Muhuri and Kushiyara also feature in the dialogue.
static.geography: India and Bangladesh share 54 rivers, most of them part of the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna (GBM) basin, which drains into the Bay of Bengal; Bangladesh is the lower riparian for almost all of them.
static.socioEconomic: Water sharing affects agriculture, inland fisheries, navigation and hydropower in both countries, and Bangladesh's heavy dependence on upstream flows makes the issue politically sensitive in Dhaka.
static.whyInNews: Uncertainty over the Ganga treaty's renewal has revived attention on the wider transboundary river agenda, including the long-pending Teesta arrangement.
static.wayForward: Basin-level planning, joint flood forecasting and real-time data exchange, and a standing dispute-resolution mechanism to reduce dependence on episodic political goodwill.
prelimsPointers: India and Bangladesh share 54 rivers.
The India-Bangladesh Joint Rivers Commission was established in 1972.
The Teesta water-sharing agreement has been pending since 2011.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why India's transboundary river agreements with neighbours have progressed slowly, and suggest institutional reforms to make water cooperation more resilient.

prelims: Ganga Waters Treaty: signed 12 December 1996 between India and Bangladesh; valid 30 years, expiring in December 2026.
Farakka Barrage, commissioned in 1975, is in Murshidabad district, West Bengal, and is the measurement point for the treaty's lean-season allocations.
Under the treaty, Bangladesh receives 35,000 cusecs when the 10-day average flow at Farakka is 75,000 cusecs or above, with the share tapering in leaner periods.
India and Bangladesh share 54 rivers; the Joint Rivers Commission was set up in 1972.
stories.mainsQuestion: The 1996 India-Bangladesh Ganga Waters Treaty is set to lapse in December 2026. Examine the factors delaying its renewal and suggest a durable framework for transboundary river cooperation in the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna basin.
